recommended_site_copy.headline: Knowledge-compiled. Browser-executed. Built for partner delivery.
recommended_site_copy.runtime_claim: A deterministic core turns client requirements into source-backed answers, editable proposals and scoped services without requiring a model call. Optional AI-assisted reading and answering is an explicit separate path.
recommended_site_copy.source_claim: Adobe-published product evidence, combined with a curated delivery catalog and implementation knowledge.
recommended_site_copy.word_claim: Word proposals are assembled locally from the answers already on the page. Export makes no model call.
recommended_site_copy.value_claim: One connected workflow carries the same service IDs, prerequisites and planning estimates from requirements through answers to a statement of work.

claims.claim: Python validates and compiles the facts and method knowledge bases, then embeds them with the catalog and JavaScript into a static browser application.
claims.qualification: This describes source/build architecture, not verification of which build is currently deployed on Adobe Proto.

claims.claim: PDF, DOCX, XLSX/XLSM, CSV and plain-text import is implemented in the browser using local parsing libraries; structured forms retain row identifiers, sections and priorities.
claims.qualification: Old .doc and .xls formats are explicitly rejected; scanned PDFs without a text layer need another input. Browser parsing is not a promise of perfect extraction for every document.

claims.claim: The core ranks catalog services using product names and aliases, explicit signals, tokenized phrase overlap, inverse document frequency, and scope/exclusion rules.
claims.qualification: Rule-based retrieval and composition; do not describe it as neural reasoning, learned embeddings, or a guarantee of universal semantic understanding.

claims.claim: The answer engine selects a lead method and eligible support methods, then assembles the client context, approach, implementation steps, deliverables, planning effort, risks, prerequisites and source links.
claims.qualification: Authored delivery methods and planning estimates are combined with Adobe-published evidence; not every sentence is an Adobe-authored statement.

claims.claim: The facts build maps supporting quotations to Adobe source URLs and titles, with normalized quote-presence checks in verified research records, a PDF or a recorded Trust Center snapshot.
claims.qualification: Quote matching checks provenance, not the truth of every inferred recommendation or perpetual source currency. Statements marked own bypass quote/source mapping.

claims.claim: The method build checks catalog service coverage, schema, step/deliverable bounds, cadence, product-name support, phrase validity and topic references; failures prevent writing the runtime knowledge base.
claims.qualification: The build prefers reviewed entries but falls back to drafts when reviewed files are absent. Do not imply every entry has independent human approval.

claims.claim: The current Word exporter assembles a DOCX in the browser from existing answers, client context, catalog services/hours and sources, using the local docx library and no inference request.
claims.qualification: This is a claim about export execution. Existing answers can include optional AI output if the partner previously selected the RFI Agent.

claims.claim: An explicit optional RFI Agent button sends document text for AI reading and applicable question context for AI answering; failed AI answers fall back to the catalog.
claims.qualification: This path uses a network service. Do not say the entire application never uses AI or that every user document always remains on device.

claims.claim: The Word builder uses the current answer for each requirement, including an answer written by the optional RFI Agent when present.
claims.qualification: Deterministic export does not retroactively make AI-written text non-AI.

claims.claim: The worker snapshot still exposes /rfi/propose; the current browser Word exporter no longer calls that route.
claims.qualification: The new runtime path removed inference from Word generation, not all AI infrastructure from the repository.

claims.claim: The RFI-to-SOW handoff uses services from answers the partner selected, deduplicates service IDs, preserves unticked prerequisites, and merges scope into existing local engagement state.
claims.qualification: This is explicit partner review and local state transfer, not an enterprise approval/audit service.

claims.claim: The canvas checks catalog product prerequisites and alternative dependencies before counting services, handles defined replacements/overlaps, and computes one-time plus monthly planning totals from selected effort and partner rates.
claims.qualification: Catalog hours are planning estimates. No evidence from this audit establishes commercial quote accuracy or market-validated rates.

claims.claim: The core SOW workflow persists engagement selections and the cross-page handoff in browser localStorage.
claims.qualification: Local browser state is not multi-user persistence, centralized access control or an audit log.

claims.claim: A current browser test downloads the real Word proposal and asserts export in under eight seconds with zero nonlocal requests; it also inspects DOCX content.
claims.qualification: Test definition inspected in this audit; not executed here. Do not report the performance assertion as measured production latency.

limitations.finding: proposalPack() still restricts context to the first five identified Adobe products; the new Word narrative iterates all Adobe questions while the services table only resolves services present in that pack. RFIs naming more than five Adobe products need review for potential narrative/services-table mismatch.
limitations.status: source-inspected potential defect; not reproduced in browser

Use no model call for core deterministic execution and current Word export, rather than no AI anywhere. AI-assisted development is a separate user-reported development fact.

commercial_model.methodology:
# Brand Visibility partner rollout: 2027 commercial model

This model makes the CRO's original question primary: **can the product help partners create more Brand Visibility business in 2027?** Brand Visibility subscription value appears first. Additional Adobe product value appears in a second stream. The two are never hidden in one headline.

All commercial inputs are illustrative, editable hypotheses. No observed partner adoption, bid-time reduction, qualified pipeline, win-rate uplift, incremental license value, attribution, margin or 2027 forecast has been supplied. The three presets are sensitivity cases, not probability bounds or an industry benchmark. A strong case is one that remains persuasive after a technical reviewer changes the inputs.

## Suggested site language

**Headline:** Give partners a faster path to more Brand Visibility business.

**Subhead:** Model the 2027 subscription revenue opportunity, then prove the assumptions in a measured partner pilot. Start with Brand Visibility. Show additional Adobe product revenue separately.

**Base-case explanation:** Under the editable base assumptions, 100 target active partners generate an estimated $399,263 of incremental Brand Visibility subscription revenue during 2027 and $798,525 of incremental annual recurring revenue at year end. This is a planning scenario, not an Adobe forecast. Its value depends on eligible opportunities, adoption, time saved, customer wins and new subscription value that can be attributed to the tool.

**Action:** Put a measured pilot in front of partners. Compare approved submission time, response quality, additional qualified bids and incremental Adobe subscriptions with the current workflow. Replace the assumptions with evidence before expanding the rollout.

**Useful short labels:** “2027 modeled BV subscription revenue”; “Year-end incremental BV ARR”; “Additional Adobe subscription revenue”; “Assumptions you can change”; “What the pilot must prove”.

If the UI uses “recognized revenue,” label it **“Modeled 2027 recognized subscription revenue”** and keep the recognition-timing assumption visible. This is a simplified service-period planning calculation, not a revenue-recognition determination.

## API and integration

`roi-model.js` is standalone, requires no DOM, has no network calls and makes no persistent changes. It exposes `window.WarroomROI` in a browser and `module.exports` in Node.

```js
const scenario = WarroomROI.portfolioPresets.base;
const result = WarroomROI.calculatePortfolio(scenario);
// Primary headline:
result.brandVisibility.adobe.modeledYearOneSubscriptionRevenue;
result.brandVisibility.adobe.modeledYearEndIncrementalARR;
// Separate expansion opportunity:
result.otherAdobe.adobe.modeledYearOneSubscriptionRevenue;
result.otherAdobe.adobe.modeledYearEndIncrementalARR;
```

`calculate(inputs)` handles one product-value stream. `presets` are the standalone Brand Visibility cases with the whole program cost assigned to BV. `portfolioPresets` put costs in one shared budget and set both stream-specific budgets to zero. This avoids charging the shared rollout twice. `calculatePortfolio(inputs)` adds shared and explicitly stream-specific costs. For a BV-first decision, `brandVisibilityInvestmentGate` compares BV contribution alone with the whole program cost. In the base case it is $299,446.88 BV contribution against $200,000 investment, a modeled $99,446.88 surplus and 49.7% BV-only contribution ROI. This gate does not charge the cost a second time in combined totals. Do not display zero-cost per-stream break-even values from the portfolio preset as an investment conclusion. `buildCostHypothesis()` handles the separate rebuild-cost illustration.

Output numbers retain precision. Round for display only. Fractional RFPs and wins are aggregate expected values, not completed documents or signed contracts. All money is USD, with no modeled foreign-exchange movement. Unknown input names, invalid rates and invalid denominators throw instead of silently changing the model.

## Input definitions

| Input | Unit and meaning | Evidence needed |
|---|---|---|
| `activePartners` | Target number of productively active firms at full deployment; not people or invitations | Named partner cohort and activation criteria |
| `opportunitiesPerPartnerYear` | Annual qualified RFP opportunities per active partner with potential incremental value for this product stream | Opportunity register, qualification and portfolio deduplication |
| `currentSubmitRate` | Fraction of those qualified opportunities submitted today, 0–1 | Baseline submitted / eligible opportunities |
| `hoursBefore`, `hoursAfter` | Total labor through approved submission, including review, rework and final scope | Timed comparable work; use total participant hours |
| `reinvestmentFraction` | Share of released hours available for extra qualified submissions, 0–1 | Staffing constraints and actual time allocation |
| `baselineWinRate` | Eventual win probability for comparable baseline opportunities, 0–1 | Mature CRM cohorts with consistent denominator |
| `winRateUpliftPp` | Absolute percentage-point change on baseline submissions; 2 means 20% becomes 22% | Matched or randomized comparison; allow negative values |
| `addedSubmissionWinRate` | Optional eventual win rate for marginal additional submissions; null uses the post-tool rate | Quality of opportunities previously declined |
| `ramp` | Productive partner exposure over the year as a fraction of full-year activation; 0.65 means 65 partner-years for 100 target partners | Monthly adoption and sustained use |
| `licenseARRPerWin` | Incremental annual subscription contract value per win in this stream, excluding existing spend and other products | Actual incremental contract lines, discounts and renewal baseline |
| `attribution` | Fraction of modeled incremental outcome causally credited to the product, 0–1 | Experimental design / documented attribution policy |
| `realization` | Share of modeled incremental outcomes whose subscriptions are active by year end | Submission-to-close and service-start dates |
| `recognitionFraction` | Average part of one subscription year delivered within the measurement year among realized outcomes, 0–1 | Service-start cohorts; Finance validation |
| `contributionMargin` | Incremental contribution after attributable delivery/selling costs, before modeled rollout budget, 0–1 | Finance-owned incremental economics; not company gross margin |
| `rolloutCost`, `annualRunBudget` | One-time rollout plus annual support/ownership/enablement costs | Costed rollout plan, including security, privacy, maintenance and measurement |
| `partnerLoadedHourlyCost` | Optional labor-equivalent value of partner capacity, not billing rate or automatic cash savings | Partner cost estimate |
| `cashSavingsFraction` | Fraction of residual labor-equivalent value with actual spend removed; default zero | Reduced contract spend, overtime or other realized expenditure |
| `delayMonths` | Number of months used in the steady-state opportunity illustration | Chosen planning comparison |
| `irrecoverableShare` | Assumed share of missed opportunity cohorts that cannot be recovered; default zero | Deadline expiry / lost-customer evidence |

Do not apply `realization` as another win probability: the win rate already models wins. It represents timing inside 2027. Do not multiply ramp twice. If the opportunity number already reflects partial activation, use ramp 1. If win rates already measure active subscriptions by the end of the same year, use realization 1 or redefine the cohort consistently. For a funded rollout, replace the annual factors with a monthly adoption, close and service-start model.

## Core calculation and accounting boundaries

Let P be target active partners, Q opportunities per partner-year, r ramp, s current submission rate, h0/h1 labor hours before/after, u reinvestment, w0 baseline win rate, d absolute win-rate change, wn added-submission win rate, A incremental annual subscription value, a attribution and z realization.

```
Eligible opportunities E = P × Q × r
Baseline submissions S0 = E × s
Hours released H = S0 × (h0 − h1)
Extra submissions ΔS = min(E − S0, max(0, H) × u / h1)
Hours spent on extra bids = ΔS × h1
Residual capacity = H − ΔS × h1

Extra wins from bid volume = ΔS × wn
Extra wins from better conversion = S0 × d
Incremental expected wins ΔW = ΔS × wn + S0 × d
Attributable year-end incremental ARR = ΔW × A × a × z
```

If the same post-tool win rate applies to both opportunity groups, wn = w0 + d. The decomposition is algebraically identical to `(S0 + ΔS) × (w0 + d) − S0 × w0`. Do not add full new wins to the win-rate improvement again. The optional marginal win rate makes it possible to assume that previously declined opportunities are harder to win.

Released hours spent on extra bids cannot also be claimed as saved labor. Only residual capacity is valued after extra submissions. Even that value is capacity until actual spend is removed. Partner capacity does not accrue to Adobe as a cost saving. Do not sum partner labor value, Adobe ARR and a rebuild-cost hypothesis.

The denominator contains only **qualified opportunities capable of producing incremental Adobe subscription value**. Count unique customer/opportunity IDs across the partner portfolio. Multiple partners bidding for one customer do not create multiple Adobe license opportunities. Exclude services-only projects, unchanged renewals, existing license commitments and customer wins that merely move Adobe business from one partner to another. New subscription value can be new-logo business or expansion above the customer's counterfactual recurring baseline; do not count a whole existing contract as expansion. “Net-new” here means incremental program-attributed subscription value relative to that counterfactual, not total-company ARR growth after all renewals, churn and currency changes. Year-end realization includes only subscriptions still active at year end; the model does not project renewals or retention beyond 2027.

## Brand Visibility and other Adobe

`calculatePortfolio` requires a separate input object for BV and other Adobe. **The BV stream contains BV subscription value only. The other-Adobe stream excludes all BV subscription value.** Partner services, one-time implementation fees and multiyear TCV belong in neither ARR stream.

Set `valueStreamsDisjoint: true` only when this dollar boundary is met. Otherwise combined dollar outputs are suppressed. The same customer may buy both BV and another product without duplicating dollars, but deal counts can overlap.

By default `cohortRelationship` is `unknown`, which suppresses the combined win-equivalent count. Use `disjoint` only for distinct opportunity cohorts. Use `overlap` with `overlappingRealizedAttributableWins` only if that overlap is measured on the same realized/attributed basis as both streams. This is a modeled win-equivalent count, not a literal count of signed contracts. Prefer not to show a total deal count on the hero. The scenario presets explicitly assume disjoint qualified opportunity cohorts and disjoint product dollars. When opportunities overlap, do not also add the streams' labor-capacity estimates: one shared proposal may serve both products. The API intentionally returns no aggregate partner-hour total.

## Revenue, contribution and break-even

Adobe defines ARR as annual subscription contract value. ARR is not cash, multiyear TCV, partner services revenue or profit. For the simplified model:

```
2027 subscription revenue proxy = year-end incremental ARR × recognitionFraction
2027 contribution = revenue proxy × incremental contributionMargin
First-year investment = rolloutCost + annualRunBudget
First-year net contribution = contribution − investment
Illustrative first-year ROI = net contribution / investment
```

Revenue depends on service commencement and contract terms. The default recognition fraction of 0.5 is a hypothetical average six months of service, not an Adobe accounting policy. The default 75% contribution margin is an unverified planning assumption, not Adobe's actual corporate or incremental margin. If either is unknown, leave it null; the model then returns no financial ROI. ARR / investment is returned only as an explicitly separate comparison ratio, never ROI.

For one stream, with fixed budget B, margin g and recognition f:

```
Required year-end incremental ARR = B / (g × f)
Required raw incremental expected wins = B / (A × a × z × g × f)
```

When wn = w0 + d, break-even uplift is `(required wins − ΔS × w0) / (S0 + ΔS)`. When wn is independently specified, it is `(required wins − ΔS × wn) / S0`. A negative threshold means the volume effect already covers the budget under those assumptions; it is not a forecast of negative uplift. An infeasible threshold is identified rather than clamped into a believable range. The optional partner break-even holds total cost fixed; recompute cost when enrollment materially changes.

Do not calculate a simple payback month as budget / annual ARR / 12. Payback requires a cumulative monthly contribution/cash schedule, service starts and costs. This annual version does not claim a payback date.

## Delay and foregone opportunity

The delay view is a steady-state sensitivity, not a countdown of money currently being lost.

```
Monthly opportunity-cohort ARR = full-adoption annual incremental wins × A × a / 12
ARR associated with delayed cohorts = monthly opportunity-cohort ARR × delayMonths
Potential permanently foregone ARR = delayed-cohort ARR × irrecoverableShare
Potential deferred ARR = delayed-cohort ARR × (1 − irrecoverableShare)
```

These dollar outputs are the **annual contract value of hypothetical opportunity cohorts**, not monthly recognized revenue. They use full assumed productive adoption and exclude the first-year ramp/realization factors; the UI must say so. Default irrecoverable share is zero. A later bid or service start can defer value without destroying the contract. Missed deadlines or lost customers may make some value unrecoverable, but that percentage needs evidence. A rigorous delay decision compares dated immediate-rollout and delayed-rollout cash/contribution cohorts.

## Separate build-cost illustration

The builder reports one person working for approximately three weeks with no incremental Adobe project spend. Label this as a builder-reported development account. It does not establish zero economic cost: labor time, existing tools and infrastructure may still have value. It is not an audited project cost ledger.

The suggested conventional-build counterfactual is 6 developers × 6 months = **36 staff-months**. A $2,000,000 project estimate implies **$55,555.56 per staff-month**, or **$666,666.67 annualized per staff member** if all costs are allocated to those 36 staff-months. That amount could include other roles, overhead, vendor margin and contingency; it is not a verified developer compensation rate or Adobe procurement quote. A salary-only benchmark cannot validate it.

Editable cost illustrations for the same 36 staff-months: $15,000 per staff-month → $540,000; $25,000 → $900,000; $55,555.56 → approximately $2 million. These are sensitivity inputs, not market benchmarks. Do not claim “$2 million saved,” “a $2 million asset,” or a quantified productivity multiple unless a like-for-like alternative, scope, staffing, duration and actual costs are independently established.

## Pilot evidence that makes the model credible

1. Instrument qualified opportunity IDs, product stream, partner, customer, submission decision and a deduplication key. Record reasons for declining a bid.
2. Time the whole approved submission process, including expertise, review, corrections and scope reconciliation. Compare equivalent requirements and quality thresholds.
3. Separate existing submissions improved by the tool from genuinely additional submissions enabled by freed capacity. Record unused capacity instead of automatically monetizing it.
4. Measure answer correctness, material scope errors and reviewer acceptance before treating faster output as commercial progress.
5. Follow opportunities to decision and subscription service start. Separate BV contract lines, other Adobe license lines, partner services, renewals and expansion.
6. Establish a matched or randomized baseline and attribution method; verify that the tool is contributing rather than selecting the easiest deals. Keep win-rate uplift at zero until supported.
7. Give source upkeep, product support, security/privacy, partner enablement and commercial measurement explicit owners and costs.

The decision can be practical now: sponsor a controlled, instrumented pilot with named partners and measurable success criteria. Technical validation supports evaluating the system; it does not establish a commercial conversion rate.

## Source use

`sources.json` records official sources for definitions and limited wage context. Commercial scenario values do not come from those sources. The BLS wage number is intentionally not used to set either the $2 million counterfactual or the partner-hour valuation. The site should not imply Adobe has endorsed or forecast these scenarios.

## Mathematical validation

Run `node roi-model.test.js`. The checks independently work through demand caps, hour conservation, added-volume versus conversion decomposition, ARR/revenue/profit boundaries, zero adoption, zero attribution, late closes, negative conversion effects, ROI break-even, unknown overlap, value boundaries and shared costs. They validate the model arithmetic and API behavior; they do not validate business inputs.
